div.p: While spatially varying coefficient (SVC) modeling is popular in applied science, its computational burden is substantial. This is especially true if a multiscale property of SVC is considered. Given this background, this study develops a Moran's eigenvector-based spatially varying coefficients (M-SVC) modeling approach that estimates multiscale SVCs computationally efficiently. This estimation is accelerated through a (i) rank reduction, (ii) pre-compression, and (iii) sequential likelihood maximization. Steps (i) and (ii) eliminate the sample size N from the likelihood function; after these steps, the likelihood maximization cost is independent of N. Step (iii) further accelerates the likelihood maximization so that multiscale SVCs can be estimated even if the number of SVCs, K, is large. The M-SVC approach is compared with geographically weighted regression (GWR) through Monte Carlo simulation experiments. These simulation results show that our approach is far faster than GWR when N is large, despite numerically estimating 2K parameters while GWR numerically estimates only 1 parameter. Then, the proposed approach is applied to a land price analysis as an illustration. The developed SVC estimation approach is implemented in the R package ''spmoran.''

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Spatial and spatiotemporal data are increasing in size. For example, remotely sensed land cover, weather, and other information are provided as high-resolution images, which consist of a massive number of cells/samples (e.g., Griffith, 2015). Socio-economic data in many countries are available by small units such as census tracts, which are, e.g., 73,057 units in the 2010 United States census. Statistics for large spatial and spatiotemporal data are increasingly important. Unfortunately, spatial statistical approaches, which have been proposed in geostatistics (e.g., Cressie, 1993) and spatial econometrics (e.g., LeSage and Pace, 2009), typically require an inversion of a dense covariance matrix whose computational complexity is O(N 3 ), where N is the sample size. These approaches are not suitable for large samples.

To overcome this limitation, large spatial data modeling has been rapidly developing. In geostatistics, sparse and low rank approaches are representative of this development; the sparse approach includes covariance tapering (Furrer et al., 2006), use of the integrated nested Laplace approximation (INLA; Lindgren et al., 2011), and the nearest neighbor Gaussian process (NNGP; Datta et al., 2016), whereas the low rank approach includes fixed rank kriging (Cressie and Johannesson, 2008), the predictive process modeling (Banerjee et al., 2008), and the multiresolution approximation (Nychka et al., 2015) (see Heaton et al., 2017 for a review). These approaches are mainly for spatial interpolation. Meanwhile, spatial econometricians have studied large data modeling mainly for regression problems in the presence of spatial dependence. For example, polynomial-based approximations (Smirnov and Anselin, 2001;Griffith, 2004), a composite likelihood approximation (Arbia, 2014), and other likelihood approximations (e.g., LeSage and Pace, 2007) have been proposed. Burden et al. (2015) proposed a low rank approach. Spatial two-stage least squares (Kelejian and Prucha, 1998) is known as a computationally efficient approach.

Although spatial dependence and spatial heterogeneity are two general properties of spatial data (Tobler, 1970;Goodchild, 2004;Anselin, 2010), these preceding studies have paid attention to the former, whereas the latter has been somewhat overlooked. Nevertheless, consideration of spatial heterogeneity is crucially important to model spatial data appropriately (see, Fotheringham et al., 2002;Geniaux and Martinetti, 2018;Debarsy and Yang, 2018).

Given this background, this study focuses on spatially varying coefficient (SVC) modeling, which is a representative approach for spatial heterogeneity modeling. Geographically weighted regression (GWR: Brunsdon et al., 1996;Fotheringham et al., 2002) and the Bayesian SVC process modeling (Gelfand et al., 2003) are representative approaches for SVC modeling (see Section 2). After Finley et al. (2011) applied the Bayesian approach to estimate multiscale SVCs, the importance of considering the multiscale property has been suggested to appropriately estimate SVCs (e.g., Fotheringham et al., 2017;Murakami et al., 2019); for example, the first SVC might have a larger-scale map pattern than the other SVCs. However, if such a multiscale property is considered, the computational cost rapidly increases depending on not only N but also the number of SVCs (see Section 2); the resulting computational cost becomes prohibitive (Finley et al., 2011). Although Harris et al. (2010A), Tran et al. (2016), and Li et al. (2018) respectively parallelized GWR for fast SVC estimation, they assume a uniform scale across SVCs. How to estimate multiscale SVCs computationally efficiently remains unclear.

The objective of this study is to overcome this limitation. Specifically, we develop an approach to estimate multiscale SVCs computationally efficiently by extending the Moran's eigenvectorspatial filtering approach (Griffith, 2003;Murakami et al., 2017Murakami et al., , 2019)). The subsequent sections are organized as follows. Section 2 briefly reviews existing SVC modeling approaches, and compares their computational properties. Section 3 introduces our SVC model, and Section 4 develops a fast SVC estimation method. Section 5 compares the computational time of the proposed approach with existing approaches through Monte Carlo simulation experiments. Section 6 presents an empirical application. Finally, Section 7 concludes our discussion.

div.head: SVC modeling approaches
div.p: Suppose that response variables y(s i ) are sampled at N sample sites s i |i ∈ {1, . . . , N}, distributed in a study region, D ⊂ R 2 . The linear SVC model is formulated as follows:
div.formula: y (s i ) = K ∑ k=1 x k (s i ) β k (s i ) + ε (s i ) , E [ε(s i )] = 0, Var [ε(s i )] = σ 2 ,(1)
div.p: where, x k (s i ) represents the kth explanatory variable, β k (s i ) represents the kth SVC, and σ 2 is a variance parameter. SVC modeling aims to estimate and infer about β k (s i ).

Geographical weighted regression (GWR; Brunsdon et al., 1996) is the representative approach for SVC modeling. GWR estimates β k (s i ) by assigning more weights on samples nearby than those far from the site s i . The estimator for β (s i ) = [β 1 (s i ) , . . . , β K (s i )] ′ , where '' ′ '' denotes the matrix transpose operator, is given as
div.formula: β (s i ) = [X ′ G(s i )X] -1 X ′ G(s i )y (2)
div.p: where X is an N × K matrix of explanatory variables, y is an N × 1 vector of response variables, and G(s i ) is an N × N diagonal matrix whose jth element g(s i , s j ) represents the weight assigned to the jth sample. g(s i , s j ) is given by a distance decay kernel. For example, Wheeler and Calder (2007) and Wheeler and Waller (2009) used the exponential kernel, g
div.formula: ( s i , s j ) = exp ( -d ( s i , s j ) /b )
div.p: , where b is the bandwidth determining the scale of the SVCs; β (s i ) have a large-scale map pattern when b is large, and a small-scale pattern when b is small. The bandwidth is estimated by minimizing the corrected Akaike Information Criterion (AICc), or minimizing the predictive error from crossvalidation (CV). GWR has widely been applied in environmental studies (e.g., Harris et al., 2010B;Dong et al., 2018), criminology (e.g., Cahill and Mulligan, 2007), epidemiology (e.g., Nakaya et al., 2005), and many other fields. The single bandwidth implicitly imposes a strong assumption that all the SVCs have the same scale of spatial variation. However, some coefficients might have a larger scale pattern than the others. To consider such a multiscale property, Yang (2014) and Fotheringham et al. (2017) proposed the flexible-band GWR (FB-GWR; also called the multiscale GWR), which replaces the common b with the SVC-specific bandwidth, b k . The FB-GWR is estimated by a back-fitting algorithm that sequentially iterates the AICc maximization (or the CV) for each b k until convergence. Recently, Lu et al. (2018) proposed a computationally efficient algorithm for FB-GWR model estimation, achieving more than a 60% reduction in computational time. Yet, because the original FB-GWR is slow even when N ≤ 5000, as we show later, a much faster algorithm might be required for larger samples.

The Bayesian SVC model (B-SVC model;Gelfand et al., 2003) furnishes another approach. This model assumes that the kth SVC, β k = [β k (s 1 ) , . . . , β k (s N )] ′ , obeys the following Gaussian process (GP):
div.formula: β k ∼ N (b k 1, τ k C (r k )) ,(3)
div.p: where b k , τ k , and r k are parameters, and 1 (N × 1) is a vector of ones. C(r k ) (N × N) is a correlation matrix whose (i, j)th element, c ij (r k ), is given by a distance decay function to capture spatial dependence, such as the exponential correlation function, c ij (r k ) = exp[-d(s i , s j )/r k ], where d(s i , s j ) is the Euclidean distance between sites s i and s j . The B-SVC model, Eqs. (1) and ( 2), is estimated by Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques. Wheeler and Waller (2009), and Finley (2011), among others, have compared the B-SVC modeling with GWR, and showed the robustness of the B-SVC approach.

Unfortunately, the computational cost for the full GP-based B-SVC modeling is disappointedly heavy when N and/or K is large Finley et al. (2011). This is because the MCMC simulation requires inverting the dense matrices C(r 1 ), . . . C(r K ) in each iteration. There are a number of studies for fast B-SVC modeling. Finley et al. (2011) approximated the GPs to model SVCs using the predictive process, which is a rank reduced GP. Datta et al. (2016) approximated the GPs using NNGP, which provides a sparse and non-degenerative approximation for GP. Beyond GP, Jaya et al. (2016) and Osei and Stein (2017) employed INLA, which is a deterministic approximation of Bayesian modeling, to estimate a conditional autoregressive process-based B-SVC model. 1 Umlauf et al. (2012) developed a structured additive regression approach, which is available to estimate a B-SVC model. 2 These Bayesian approaches are robust and provide full statistical inference from large samples for SVCs.

Yet, these fast approximations can be slow for very large N. For example, the NNGP-based approach took 41.35 h to estimate 2 SVCs from 114,371 observations (Datta et al., 2016). Even for a few thousand observations, computation can be slow if K is large. For example, the predictive process-based approach with 50,000 MCMC iterations, which was coded in C++ and Fortran, requires ∼72 h when N = 8774 and K = 5 (Finley et al., 2011B). A faster approach that works within minutes even with larger N and K is more preferable in practice.

A Moran eigenvector SVC (M-SVC) modeling approach (Griffith, 2008), which is an extension of the Moran eigenvector spatial filtering approach (see Griffith, 2003;Griffith and Chun, 2014), furnishes another option for multiscale SVC modeling. While instability of this approach was alluded to by Helbich and Griffith (2016), Oshan and Fotheringham (2018) and Murakami et al. (2017Murakami et al. ( , 2019) ) extended it to approximate the B-SVC model, and Murakami et al. (2017Murakami et al. ( , 2019) ) demonstrated its estimation accuracy through Monte Carlo experiments. Unlike the typical B-SVC modeling approach, their approach does not require MCMC iterations. Regardless, it is still slow when N is large because it requires an eigen-decomposition (complexity: O(N 3 )) and numerical estimation of 2K parameters.

Thus, how to estimate multiscale SVCs computationally efficiently remains elusive. Because SVC modeling is popular in a wide variety of applied fields, achieving fast computation without relying on high performance computing environment is desirable.

Eγ 1 is the term to capture residual spatial dependence. Murakami and Griffith (2018) showed that the term Eγ 1 with L = 200 greatly reduces residual spatial dependence.
The kth SVC is parameterized as follows:
div.formula: β k = b k 1 + Eγ k , γ k ∼ N(0, τ 2 k Λ α k ),(6)
div.p: where b k is a coefficient. The SVC consists of the constant term b k 1 and the spatially varying term Eγ k . The term Eγ k has the following properties: (i) it is interpretable in terms of the MC; and, (ii) the eigenvectors have zero means. Property (i) is important to model spatial dependence variations accurately as discussed. Property (ii) is required to make the mean term, b k 1, and Eγ k identifiable (see, Gelfand et al., 2003).

Vector γ k contains random coefficients that depend on two shrinkage parameters, τ k 2 and α k . Parameter τ k 2 controls the variance of the spatial variation of β k . Parameter α k controls the spatial scale; large α k shrinks coefficients on minor eigen-pairs with small eigenvalues, and the resulting SVCs have a large-scale map pattern. The opposite is true for small α k . Thus, α k estimates the scale of the SVCs instead of the range parameter, which we consider as fixed. This replacement enables drastically accelerating model estimation while maintaining flexibility in estimating the scale. Murakami and Griffith (2018) showed that the estimation error is small when α k rather than r is estimated.

div.head: Fast M-SVC modeling
div.p: Unfortunately, the Moran eigenvector approach is computationally inefficient in terms of both modeling and estimation. Section 4.1 presents how to reduce the cost for modeling, whereas Section 4.2 presents how to reduce the cost for estimation.

div.head: Modeling
div.p: The cost for the eigen-decomposition of (I -11 ′ /N)C(I -11 ′ /N) is O(N 3 ), which is intractable for large N. Besides, if C is given using a distance-decay function like in our case, the N × N matrix must be stored before the decomposition. The modeling is inefficient in terms of both computational complexity and memory usage.

To address these problems, we apply a Nystrom extension (Drineas and Mahoney, 2005) based approximation of Moran eigenvectors and eigenvalues (Murakami and Griffith, 2018) that is formulated as follows 3 :

where '' ⨂ '' denotes the Kronecker product operator. C L is a L × L spatial proximity matrix with L knots (L ≪ N) distributed across the study region. The knots are given by the k-means cluster centers calculated using the spatial coordinates of sample sizes (see Zhang and Kwok, 2010). 4 C NL (N × L) is a proximity matrix between the L knots and the N sample sites. The set {E L , Λ L , I L , 1 L } is defined just like the set {E, Λ, I, 1} for the knots.

Following Murakami and Griffith (2018), which shows that 200 eigen-pairs are sufficient to model spatial dependence, L is fixed by the number of positive eigenvalues in Λ if it is below 200, and 200 otherwise. Given that L is fixed, the computational complexity for the eigen-approximation yields O(N), whereas the memory usage yields N × L. However, most studies have assumed at most 10 SVCs, partly due to the difficulty of identifying SVCs (see Wheeler and Tiefelsdorf, 2005;Farber and Páez, 2007;Helbich and Griffith, 2016). Identifiability can be improved by replacing some of the SVCs with constant coefficients (Mei et al., 2004;Nakaya et al., 2009).

Thus, we assume that L is fixed and K ≪ N. When a large number of explanatory variables must be considered, SVCs can be given only for some focused explanatory variables, whereas constant coefficients are assumed for the others. The kth SVC is substituted by a constant coefficient by
div.formula: replacing β k = b k 1 + Eγ k with b k 1.
div.p: This property is useful to avoid increasing the number of SVCs, and to assure their identifiability.

div.head: Estimation
div.p: The likelihood maximization can be very slow because it includes 2K shrinkage parameters in Θ ∈ {θ 1 , . . . , θ K }, where θ k ∈ {τ k , α k }, that do not have closed form solutions. For example, if 10 SVCs are assumed, 20 shrinkage parameters must be estimated numerically. The M-SVC model estimation is much more difficult than GWR, which numerically estimates 1 bandwidth, or FB-GWR, which estimates K bandwidths. This section shows that the computational cost for the M-SVC model estimation is drastically reduced by employing selected matrix tricks. Section 4.2.1 eliminates N from the likelihood function, and Section 4.2.2 derives a sequential approach to maximize the likelihood.

div.head: Summary
div.p: Our approach is summarized in Fig. 1. In the modeling step, we apply (i) a rank reduction, and each SVC is expressed as a linear combination of L approximate eigenvectors Ê (N × L). In the estimation step, we first apply (ii) a pre-compression, and the SVCs are compressed into K 2 (L + 1) 2 + K +1 inner products that appear in step (a) in Section 4.2.1. Owing to this step, the computational cost for the likelihood evaluation is independent of N. Furthermore, the likelihood maximization is accelerated by (iii) a sequential estimation. The estimation in (iii) iterates processing of O(L 3 ). Because the cost is independent of N, the estimation is fast even if N is very large. Yet, the computational cost increases as K grows. This outcome is because large K increases the number of iterations to estimate θ 1 , . . . θ K sequentially. The computational cost can be reduced by applying SVCs only on some focused explanatory variables, as explained before.

div.head: Monte Carlo simulation experiment
div.p: This section compares our approach with existing approaches in terms of computational time and estimation accuracy. We executed four simulation experiments. The first experiment, whose results are summarized in Section 5.1, compared our approach with the original M-SVC, GWR, and FB-GWR approaches assuming N ≤ 4000. Section 5.2 summarizes results from two simulations. The first simulation compared (relatively) fast approaches, including GWR and M-SVC, assuming 6000 ≤ N ≤ 12,000. Another experiment with results summarized in Section 5.2 examined performance of our approach with larger samples (20,000 ≤ N ≤ 100,000). Besides, Section 5.3 reports experimental results focusing on statistical inference. Throughout Section 5, we use a Mac Pro (3.5 GHz, 6-Core Intel Xeon E5 processor with 64 GB memory). R (version 3.6.2; https://cran.r-project.org/) is used for the model estimation. The package GWmodel (version 2-0.5; see Lu et al., 2014B) is used to estimate GWR and FB-GWR models. Note that the FB-GWR is not the fast version recently proposed by Lu et al. (2018).

div.head: Result
div.p: This section first quantifies influence from the following three approximations: (i) the eigenapproximation, (ii) the pre-compression, and (iii) the sequential estimation.

Regarding (i), the original M-SVC model (M-SVC) and our M-SVC with the eigen-approximation (M-SVC (i) ) are compared. Fig. 2 portrays RMSEs and biases. Solid and dotted lines represent the results from M-SVC (i) and the original M-SVC, respectively. These figures show that their RMSEs and biases are almost the same. Fig. 3 shows the mean correlation coefficients between SVCs estimated with the two approaches. The smallest value of 0.985 occurs when N = 500 and K = 8. The correlation coefficients increase as N increases, and the values are greater than 0.997 in all cases when N = 4000. These results confirm that the error due to (i) the Moran's eigenvector approximation is quite small. The computational gain by the approximation is substantial. Because the computational cost for the eigen-decomposition increases rapidly -it is of the order of N 3 -the original M-SVC approach is not feasible for large samples, say N > 10,000. The cost for our eigen-approximation, which is based on the Nystrom extension (see Murakami and Griffith, 2018), increases only linearly with respect to N; it is available for large samples. In summary, the eigen-approximation considerably accelerates computation with a small approximation error.

Regarding (ii), the pre-compression, and (iii), the sequential estimation, we compare M-SVC (i) , M-SVC (ii) using (i)-(ii), and M-SVC (iii) using (i)-(iii). Because of the computational burden here, the simulations employ only 20 iterations.

Figs. 4 and 5 compare bias and RMSE between M-SVC (i) /M-SVC (ii) and M-SVC (iii) . 6 Each approach indicates similar bias and RMSE values. Bias is small across cases. RMSE decreases as N increases and K decreases. Fig. 6 plots the minimum (i.e., the worst) correlation coefficients between the SVC estimates of M-SVC (i) /M-SVC (ii) and M-SVC (iii) . The minimum value results in 0.958 when N = 500 and K = 8. When 1000 ≤ N, the value is always greater than 0.990. It is verified that the error introduced by (iii), the sequential estimation, is quite small, whereas (ii) does not produce any error. Besides, the correlation coefficients summarized in Figs. 3 and 6 reveal that the SVCs estimated with the original M-SVC and our M-SVC (iii) are almost the same. This result implies that the accuracy of the M-SVC approach, which is better than the standard GWR and the same as FB-GWR, holds for M-SVC (iii) (see, Murakami and Griffith, 2018).

Fig. 7 compares computational times of M-SVC (i) , M-SVC (ii) , M-SVC (iii) , GWR, and FB-GWR. Unlike classical GWR, the computational times of M-SVC and FB-GWR rapidly increase as K grows. This outcome highlights the difficulty of estimating multiscale SVCs when K is large.

M-SVC (i) is the slowest when K ≥ 6, whereas FB-GWR is the slowest when K ≤ 4. Although M-SVC (ii) is faster than M-SVC (i) , it is still slow. For example, when N = 4000 and K = 8, M-SVC (ii) took 2903 s and M-SVC (i) took 5270 s. These results indicate that (i), the eigen-approximation, and (ii), the pre-compression, are not sufficient for fast SVC estimation. However, M-SVC (iii) is considerably faster than either M-SVC (i) or M-SVC (ii) . When N = 4000 and K = 8, its estimation took 453.6 s on average. Yet, it is slower than GWR, which took only 195.1 s on average in the same case.

div.head: Simulation with large samples (5000 ≤ N ≤ 100,000) 5.2.1. Simulation settings
div.p: This section compares estimation accuracy and computational time for M-SVC (iii) , which was found to be accurate and relatively fast when N is small, with those for GWR using large samples. FB-GWR is not compared because it is computationally too expensive for large N. The large synthetic data are generated with Eqs. ( 27) and ( 28):
div.formula: y = K ∑ k=1 x k • β k + ε, ε ∼ N ( 0, σ 2 I ) ,(27)
β k = 1 + Ê+ γ k , γ k ∼ N ( 0, Λα k + ) .(28)
div.p: where x k is randomly generated from N(0, I) if k > 1, and
div.formula: x k = 1 if k = 1.
div.p: To generate SVCs within a reasonable time frame, β k is generated from Ê+ γ k , where Ê+ is a N × L + matrix of Moran eigenvectors corresponding to positive eigenvalues, and Λ+ is a L + × L + diagonal matrix of the positive eigenvalues (i.e., λl > 0). Ê+ and Λ+ are generated as follows: (a) eigen-pairs for the L knots are generated from Eqs. ( 12) and ( 13) using C L , which is the 2000 × 2000 matrix whose (i, j)th element equals exp(-d(s i , s j )); and, (b) eigen-pairs corresponding to λ ≤ 0 are eliminated. Thus, β k is given by a positively dependent spatial process using at most 2000 eigenvectors corresponding to λl > 0. Our preliminary analysis showed that the number of eigenvalues satisfying λ > 0 is almost always less than 2000 even when N = 100,000. In other words, the assumption of a maximum of 2000 eigenvectors is reasonable considering the cost for computation. Note that the 2000 eigenvectors are used only for data generation; as before, at most, 200 eigenvectors are used for the M-SVC model estimation.

The α k parameter determines the spatial scale of β k . To test the influence of scale on estimation accuracy, assume α k = 2, which represents a large scale, for the first K /2 SVCs, and α k = 0.5, which represents a small scale, for the remaining K /2 SVCs.
Hereafter, Section 5.2.2 compares M-SVC (iii) and GWR assuming N ≤ 12,000. Section 5.2.3 applies M-SVC (iii) to larger samples. In both sections, estimation involves 200 iterations in each case.

div.head: Result ( N ≤ 12,000)
div.p: This section compares M-SVC (iii) to GWR assuming N ∈ {6000, 9000, 12,000} and K ∈ {2, 4, 6, 8}. Fig. 8 portrays the mean bias for the large-scale SVCs (left) and the small-scale SVCs (right). This result shows that the biases are quite small irrespective of scale. Fig. 9 displays the mean RMSEs. This result shows that the RMSE of M-SVC (iii) is considerably smaller than that for GWR if SVCs have a large-scale map pattern. Actually, as illustrated by Fig. 10, M-SVC (iii) estimates large-scale SVCs almost perfectly, whereas GWR estimates have somewhat noisy patterns relative to the true values. The result is reasonable because M-SVC (iii) uses the first L eigenvectors describing the L largest-scale map patterns explained by the Moran coefficient (see Griffith, 2003).
Despite that M-SVC (iii) considers only the L large-scale eigenvectors, accuracy of M-SVC (iii)

estimates for small-scale β k is still better than estimates from GWR. This might be because M-SVC (iii) estimates the scale α k for each β k , whereas GWR estimates a common scale/bandwidth for all β k s. One finding is that M-SVC (iii) declines in accuracy as N increases. This is because M-SVC (iii) limits L to no more than 200 (see Section 4.1), and these 200 eigenvectors explain largescale variations. Overcoming this limitation is an important future task. Still, true small-scale SVCs and those estimated by M-SVC (iii) are visually quite similar (Fig. 10), whereas GWR estimates tend to be smoother than the true distribution, probably due to its assumption of the same scale across
div.formula: β k s.
div.p: Thus, the accuracy of M-SVC (iii) is verified as least when N ≤ 12,000. A comparison of computational time is summarized in the next subsection.

div.head: Result (N ≤ 100,000)
div.p: The previous subsection shows that accuracy of M-SVC (iii) for small-scale β k decreases as N increases. To clarify whether M-SVC (iii) estimates remain accurate and computationally tractable for larger samples, we performed another simulations with N ∈ {20,000, 40,000, 70,000, 100,000} and K ∈ {2, 4, 6, 8}, assuming the same data generating process used for Section 5.2.2. 12, the correlation coefficient between large-scale SVC estimates and the true values are very close to 1.00, which confirms the estimation accuracy. Actually, as illustrated in Fig. 13, true large-scale SVCs and the estimates are visually indistinguishable.

Regarding the small-scale SVCs with α k = 0.5, estimation accuracy decreases as N increases because of the fixed L, as previously explained. However, the RMSE increase is quite small when 40,000 ≤ N. As a result, the mean correlation coefficient between the true and estimated SVCs is approximately 0.83, even when N = 100,000. Owing to the large size of N, estimation accuracy conceivably is almost the same even if the number of SVCs, K, is increased to 8. Fig. 13 visually demonstrates that M-SVC successfully estimates small-scale patterns that are similar to the true values. These outcomes verified that our approach estimates both large-and small-scale SVCs with reasonable accuracy, even if N is large. However, the estimated SVCs are slightly smoother than the true values. Mitigating this problem while saving computational time is an important next step.

Finally, Fig. 14 summarizes computational time for GWR and M-SVC (iii) . Although GWR is fast for small samples, as shown in Section 5.1.2, its computational time rapidly increases as N grows because of the bandwidth optimization involved.

In contrast, an increase in computational time is surprisingly slow in the case of M-SVC (iii) . For example, when K = 8, if N is increased from 9000 to 100,000, the mean computational time increases from 534 s to 835 s. This computational efficiency is because our approach processes N samples in (i), the eigen-approximation, and (ii), the pre-compression steps, but these steps are required only one time, and their both of computational costs are O(N). This is the reason why the computational time increase is linear and slow. Although these linear increases explain the cost for (i) and (ii), the computational time that is needed independent of N explains the cost for (iii), the sequential estimation. Based on Fig. 14, the computational time for (iii) is around 500 s across cases when K = 8. Thus, the computational cost for (iii), the estimation, is also quite small despite this step needing to numerically estimate 16 parameters {θ 1 , . . . θ 8 }, whereas GWR numerically optimizes only 1 bandwidth parameter. Therefore, M-SVC (iii) is found to be accurate enough and extremely fast.

div.head: Simulation for statistical inference
div.p: Test of statistical significance is needed to interpret estimated SVCs appropriately. This section analyzes property of M-SVC (iii) focusing on statistical testing.

div.head: Simulation settings
div.p: We examine how accurately M-SVC (iii) , which considers only 200 eigen-pairs, approximates the full model defined by Eqs. ( 27) and ( 28), in terms of statistical testing of the null hypothesis
div.formula: β k (s i ) = 0.
div.p: Here, the test result obtained from the full model with true shrinkage and variance parameters is regarded as true. 7 The Type I error rate and statistical power are evaluated by comparing the test result of M-SVC (iii) with the true result. The Type I error rate represents the rate that M-SVC (iii) mistakenly rejects β k (s i ) = 0 when it is true (i.e., true negative). Statistical power is the rate that M-SVC (iii) properly rejects β k (s i ) = 0 when it is not true (i.e., false positive).
We performed the simulations with N ∈ {1,000, 4,000, 9,000, 20,000} and K ∈ {2, 4, 6, 8}. Based on a preliminary result that the noise variance changes test results, the variance σ 2 is given by σ
div.formula: 2 rat Var [ ∑ K k=1 x k • β k ]
div.p: , with σ 2 rat ∈ {0.5, 1.0}. The other parameter values and the data generating process are the same as before.

div.head: Results
div.p: Fig. 15 portrays the mean bias of the estimated standard errors (SEs), SE
div.formula: [ βk (s i ) ] = √ Var [ βk (s i ) ]
div.p: (see Section 3.2). SEs for the large-scale SVCs have small bias across cases. Regarding the SEs for small-scale SVCs, their bias decreases when the sample size increases from 1000 to 4000. However, when N > 4000, the SEs have a downward bias that grows as N increases. This bias is attributable to the rank reduction that ignores small-scale variations. Reducing this bias by applying a bias-correction (Finley et al., 2009) or extending the procedure to a scalable approach (e.g., Katzfuss, 2017) is an important future research topic. Fig. 16 displays the Type I error rates for the estimated SVCs. The significance level of 5% is used for the evaluation. The error rates for the large-scale SVCs are less than 0.19 across cases. This rate 7 In this type of simulation experiment, the more common design is to generate synthetic data under a null hypothesis and fit a model to evaluate the Type I rate and/or statistical power. If we follow this routine, we need to generate the simulation data while assuming β k (s i ) = 0 for some sites, and β k (s i ) ̸ = 0 for the other sites. However, such spatial inhomogeneity in the SVCs is inconsistent with our modeling assumption that SVCs have homogeneous spatial processes explained by the MEs. Although the SVCs become homogeneous if β k (s i ) = 0 is assumed at all the sites, this assumption is too restrictive. Because of these reasons, we did not employ this typical routine. decreases as N increases. This outcome confirms that our statistical testing is credible if the SVCs have large-scale variations. If N ≤ 4000, the same is true for small-scale SVCs; their Type I error rates are less than 0.18 across cases. In contrast, because of the downward bias of the SEs, the error rate gradually increases as N increases, especially in cases with small noise and a small number of SVCs. The importance of mitigating this downward bias of the SEs is suggested again to avoid Type I error.

Fig. 17 summarizes the statistical power of the estimated SVCs. This power is more than 0.93 across cases. In other words, M-SVC (iii) appropriately rejects β k (s i ) = 0 with a probability of more than 93% when β k (s i ) is truly non-zero.

Finally, Fig. 18 shows the rate that M-SVC (iii) indicates the same test with the true model; i.e., the rate that both indicate the statistical significance at the 5% level, or both indicate non-significance. This figure demonstrates that M-SVC (iii) achieves more than 87% accuracy in statistical testing. Statistical significance of SVCs is usually assessed visually by mapping statistical significance, as is done in the next section. Based on the result, the significance map obtained from M-SVC (iii) is visually similar to the true significance map.

In summary, although our approach tends to overestimate the statistical significance of smallscale SVCs when N is large, due to the underestimation of their SEs, the overall accuracy is more than 87%, and will be acceptable if the test result is interpreted not for individually locations, but through mapping of statistical significance.

div.head: An empirical study
div.p: As an illustration, GWR and M-SVC the Tokyo railway station (Tokyo_d) [km], share of green area in 1km grids (Green), and anticipated flooding depth (Flood) [m]

. We include distance-based covariates (Station_d and Tokyo_d), which can confound with SVCs and make the model estimation unstable (see Paciorek, 2010), to examine the stability of GWR and M-SVC (iii) . These data were obtained from the National Land Numerical Information download service (http://nlftp.mlit.go.jp/ksj-e/index.html), provided by MLIT, Japan.

Figs. 19 and 20 plot estimated coefficients (except for spatially varying intercepts) and their statistical significances, respectively. GWR took 721 s for its estimation, while the M-SVC approach took 241 s. The SVCs estimated with GWR have similar scales for their spatial patterns. In contrast, SVCs estimated with our M-SVC approach have considerably different scales for their spatial patterns; specifically, the SVCs for Tokyo_d have a large-scale spatial pattern, the SVCs for Forest have a moderate-scale pattern, and those for Station_d and Flood have small-scale patterns. Because Tokyo_d and Station_d can be viewed as global and local-measures of accessibility, large-and smallscale spatial patterns in these SVC estimates are intuitively reasonable. The statistical significance estimated from our approach is considerably smaller than GWR. Thus, while GWR and the M-SVC approach can yield different test results because assumptions underlying these approaches are quite different, our approach is more parsimonious than GWR. Regarding the M-SVC approach, the SVC estimates for Tokyo_d have statistically significant negative impacts in the central Tokyo and the surrounding areas; this suggests that accessibility to Tokyo encourages urbanization. Coefficients for Station_d reveal that station access has a statistically significant negative relationship with land price across the region. The significance level is especially high in suburban residential areas. SVCs for Forest show that green areas have significant negative relationships in suburban non-urban areas. Exceptionally, Forest is positively significant in the center of Tokyo. This result suggests that greening increases the attractiveness of the center. Finally, SVCs for Flood have a significant negative relationship around the Arakawa river, which is a principal river in this area. It suggests that flood risk is appropriately reflected in land prices in the Arakawa coastal areas. Flood risk also is reflected appropriately near the Narita international airport. In contrast, GWR estimates seem less interpretable because of their same scale across SVCs.
In conclusion, the M-SVC approach provides reasonable estimates and statistical significance of multiscale SVCs.

div.head: Future directions
div.p: While large spatial data modeling is a recent hot topic, related discussions are quite limited when it comes to SVC modeling. Given this background, this study develops a fast M-SVC approach that estimates multiscale SVCs. We achieve the computational efficiency using (i) rank reduction, (ii) pre-compression, and (iii) sequential estimation. Monte Carlo simulation experiments confirm the estimation accuracy and computational efficiency of our approach. Our approach estimates SVCs in relatively little time, without applying any parallel computation. In other words, a high performance computing environment is not needed for our approach.

Nevertheless, step (i) is easily parallelized, similar to the other Nystrom extension-based eigenapproximation approaches (see Li et al., 2015). The same holds for step (ii), which simply calculates inner-products. Although parallelizing the sequential estimation step (iii) is not straightforward, its computational cost is independent of N. Thus, parallelization of our approach allows ever faster estimation of multiscale SVCs, and extends results summarized here to millions of samples.

One drawback of our approach is its incapability of modeling fine-scale spatial variations, as illustrated in Fig. 13; we consider at most 200 eigenvectors corresponding to large eigenvalues, which implies ignoring the other eigenvectors that explain small-scale variations. Such a limitation in low rank spatial modeling is reported in geostatistsics (Stein, 2014). Addressing this problem is an important future research topic. Fortunately, a number of multiscale approaches have been proposed for this problem (e.g., Sang and Huang, 2012;Nychka et al., 2015).

Local approaches are more suitable than rank reduction approaches, including ours, to capture fine-scale variations (Stein, 2014). In this respect, acceleration of GWR is a sensible way to estimate fine-scale SVCs with large samples. Considering the similar estimation accuracy for the M-SVC and FB-GWR approaches (see Murakami and Griffith, 2018), acceleration of FB-GWR, GWR with parametric-specific distance matrices (PSDM-GWR; Lu et al., 2017), and other extended GWRs, also is a promising way to develop fast and flexible SVC modeling approaches. Studies about fast GWR include Harris et al. (2010A), Tran et al. (2016), Lu et al. (2017Lu et al. ( , 2018)), and Li et al. (2018).

Although we develop a fast approach for SVC estimation, the same approach potentially is available to other mixed effects model, which can be written as Eq. ( 7); they include spatial (or non-spatial) additive models, and multilevel models, among others. Extension of our fast estimation framework to a wide variety of spatial regression models would be valuable in the era of big spatial data.

Extensions also are needed to overcome limitations of our approach. For example, determining which coefficients should be spatially varying and which should be constant is important. Mei et al. (2004) and Nakaya et al. (2009) developed SVC selection procedures for GWR, and the latter implemented their approach in GWR 4.0 (http://gwr.maynoothuniversity.ie/gwr4-software/). Development of such a SVC selection procedure for our approach would be helpful to stabilize the SVC estimation. 8 Data/covariates configuration is also an important issue. Given K covariates, there are 2 K patterns in the covariate selection; a sensible combination of the covariates must be selected in a reasonable time scale. It also is needed to select appropriate distance measures to model SVCs (Lu et al., 2017). For example, travel time or network distance might be more appropriate than Euclidean distance to model SVCs for socio-economic variables (Lu et al., 2014A). Such variable selection is important in the presence of many covariates, which is usual in recent years when a wide variety of spatial data are available owing to the development of geographic information systems and sensor technologies.
The M-SVC modeling approach is implemented in an R packages ''spmoran'' (https://cran.r-proj ect.org/web/packages/spmoran/index.html; see, Murakami, 2018).
